what: Fleetio is **fleet management software**. A fleet keeps a record for every vehicle and piece of equipment in it, and uses that record to plan and document maintenance. Fleetio calls these records **vehicles** (or assets) and lets teams work in a web browser or on phones and tablets through its mobile app, **Fleetio Go**.
Think of it as the fleet's maintenance memory. It answers questions like *What's wrong with unit 214? When was its last PM? What did we spend on it this year? Which trucks are overdue?*

callout.title: Where Fleetio fits
callout.text: Fleetio is a maintenance-and-records system — a kind of [[CMMS]]. It is not a dispatch system ([[TMS]]) and it is not a GPS tracker. It can, however, pull data such as odometer readings and engine fault codes in from telematics providers like Samsara through integrations.

why: Without a system, maintenance lives in paper folders, spreadsheets and people's memory. Things get missed: a PM goes overdue, a defect from last week's inspection never gets fixed, nobody can say what a truck has cost.

tiles.title: Nothing slips
tiles.text: Service reminders flag work that is due soon or overdue, by miles, engine hours or time.

tiles.title: One history per unit
tiles.text: Every completed repair becomes part of the vehicle's service history.

tiles.title: Real costs
tiles.text: Work orders break costs into parts and labor lines, so cost per unit can be reported.

tiles.title: Defects get closed
tiles.text: Failed inspection items become issues that stay open until someone resolves them.

What they typically do in Fleetio

Reviews costs, overdue PMs and reports; sets up service programs and approval rules.
Works assigned issues and work orders, records labor and parts used.
Manages parts inventory and stock levels.
Submits inspections and reports problems from the mobile app; may log fuel.

callout.text: Exactly who does what depends on how each company sets Fleetio up. Learn your company's rules: who may open work orders, who approves costs, who closes issues.

how: Fleetio connects four kinds of information around every vehicle: **what's planned** (service reminders), **what's wrong** (issues and faults), **the work done** (work orders and service entries) and **what it cost** (parts, labor and fuel).

how.title: Everything in Fleetio hangs off the vehicle record

how: When a work order is completed, Fleetio creates a service entry from it. Both kinds of record add to the vehicle's service history and update its service reminders, so the next PM due date moves forward on its own — as long as the meter reading on the record is right.
example: **Example fleet (fictional): 60 tractors, 140 dry vans, one in-house shop.** It is Monday morning.

dialog: 06:10 — Driver Luis submits his pre-trip inspection for T-214 in Fleetio Go.
Item failed: "Lights — left low beam out", with a photo. An issue is opened on T-214.
I see the failed item on T-214. Is it only the low beam, or the high beam too?
Only the low beam. Everything else passed.
You open T-214's record. Its PM A reminder is "due soon": 1,400 miles left.
Bring it to the shop at 07:00. They'll do the headlamp and the PM A together, so you're only stopped once.

example: You create **one work order** for T-214 with two line items, the PM A service and the headlamp issue, and assign it to the shop. When the technician finishes, they record parts and labor and the work order is completed. The headlamp issue is resolved, PM A's next due point moves forward, and both jobs appear in the service history.
role: A coordinator usually works in Fleetio every day. Those tasks fall into three groups:

ul: Open issues on each vehicle, including failed inspection items and imported faults
Service reminders that are **due soon** or **overdue**
Open work orders, their status and who they are assigned to
Each vehicle's meters, assignment, service history and costs
Low-stock parts (if your fleet uses the parts module)
Work orders, with a line item for each job, plus vendor, parts and labor
Service entries for outside vendor repairs, matched to the invoice
Meter readings, whenever they aren't imported automatically
Clear notes: complaint, cause, correction, and who approved it
Invoice or estimate attachments and photos
Is the meter reading realistic? A typo like 41,288 instead of 412,880 breaks reminders and cost per mile.
Is the work on the **right unit**: tractor or trailer?
Were the related issues resolved when the work was done?
Did the next PM due point move forward after the PM was completed?
Do parts and labor totals match the vendor invoice?

items.sub: **Issue** = unplanned problem (a leak, a lamp out). **Service task** = a defined job, often planned and recurring (oil change, PM).
**Work order** = detailed job with parts/labor lines, good for planning shop work. **Service entry** = quick summary log, good for outside vendor work. A completed work order creates a service entry.

no.title: Common mistakes
items: Typing a wrong meter reading, which throws off every reminder and cost-per-mile figure
Logging trailer work on the tractor that was pulling it
Leaving the issue open after the repair is done, so it looks unresolved forever
Opening a second work order for a unit that already has one open
Fixing the defect but ignoring the PM due next week, so the truck stops twice
Writing notes like "fixed truck" with no complaint, cause or correction

Write notes someone else can understand a year from now

exercise.prompt: Trailer V-5502's driver fails the inspection item "Tires: right rear outer, sidewall bulge". The trailer is loaded and due out in 40 minutes. What do you do first in Fleetio and with the team?

options.text: Log a service entry saying the tire was replaced, so the record is complete before the trailer leaves
options.why: Never record work that hasn't happened. Records must reflect reality.

options.text: Treat it as safety-critical: hold the trailer and tell dispatch. Turn the failed item into a work order on V-5502 (the trailer, not the tractor) and arrange a tire replacement
options.why: A sidewall bulge can mean the tire is about to fail. Hold the unit, record the work on the correct unit, and arrange the repair.

options.text: Wait until the trailer's next PM and fix it then, because the issue is already recorded
options.why: Recording a problem is not fixing it. Safety-critical defects are handled before the unit moves.

ul: Fleetio is a **maintenance and fleet-records system**, not a dispatch system or a GPS tracker.
Issues are unplanned problems. Service tasks and service reminders are the planned, preventive side.
Work orders hold the detail (parts and labor lines). Completed work flows into the **service history** and updates reminders.
Records are only as good as the data: correct unit, correct meter, issues resolved, clear notes.
Combine due-soon PMs with repairs so a unit stops once instead of twice.

what: Samsara is a **[[Telematics|telematics]]** company. It calls its platform **connected operations**. Hardware installed in the vehicle collects data and sends it over the cellular network to Samsara's cloud, where the fleet sees it in a web dashboard and the drivers use the **Samsara Driver App**.

tiles.title: Vehicle Gateway
tiles.text: Samsara describes it as a cellular gateway with GPS and a CAN bus interface. It reads location and engine data.

tiles.title: AI Dash Cams
tiles.text: Road-facing and multi-camera options that record safety events and detect risky behaviors.

tiles.title: Driver App
tiles.text: Used by drivers for Hours of Service (ELD), DVIR inspections and other workflows.

tiles.title: Cloud dashboard
tiles.text: Where the office sees maps, alerts, reports, safety events, faults and maintenance.

why: Before telematics, the office knew where a truck was or what was wrong with it only when the driver called. Telematics turns every truck into a live data source.

ul: **Visibility**: where every vehicle, trailer and asset is, right now.
**Safety**: harsh driving events and AI-detected behaviors feed driver coaching.
**Compliance**: electronic logging of Hours of Service and digital DVIRs.
**Maintenance**: engine fault codes and driver-reported defects reach the maintenance team quickly.
**Cost**: fuel use and idle time show where money is wasted.

how.title: From the truck to a fleet decision

how: The gateway connects to the truck's diagnostic network (Samsara mentions a CAN bus interface), so it can read what the truck's own computers report, such as fault codes and engine data. It adds its own GPS position. Dash cams add video and AI detection. The Driver App adds HOS logs and inspections. All of this lands in one dashboard, where **alert rules** decide who gets notified.

callout.title: Telematics reports, people decide
callout.text: Samsara can show that a fault code is active. It cannot inspect the truck. A code tells you what the truck's computer detected, not always what the repair is. Talk to the driver and get a qualified technician to diagnose it.

example: **Example fleet (fictional), Tuesday 06:40.** You receive a Samsara alert email.

dialog: Alert: T-311 — engine fault code active. Location: I-80 EB, near mile 142. Moving at 61 mph.
Morning Ray, this is maintenance. Your truck reported an engine fault. Do you have any warning lamps, and does it feel any different?
The check engine light came on about ten minutes ago. Power feels normal, no other lights.
You check the fault details and suggested action steps in Samsara. Ray has 6 h 10 min of driving time left on his HOS clock.
Okay. Keep going carefully and call me right away if a red stop lamp comes on or you lose power. I'm finding a shop near your delivery so we can get it checked this afternoon.

example: Samsara gave you the fault, the location and the driver's available hours **before** the driver called. You still talked to the driver, judged urgency from their symptoms, and planned a diagnosis that fits the load.
role: Samsara monitors far more than a maintenance coordinator needs to act on. Know which signals are yours and which belong to someone else.

role.title: What Samsara monitors vs what you act on
head: Samsara shows…
Usually owned by
Does the coordinator act?
rows: **Yes.** Triage it: call the driver, read the details, decide urgency, arrange diagnosis.
**Yes.** A reported defect must be reviewed and repaired (or certified as not needing repair) per procedure.
**Uses it.** Find the nearest qualified shop or mobile service for a breakdown.
**Uses it.** Plan repair timing around the driver's legal hours.
**Usually no.** If the driver reports a mechanical cause (such as brakes pulling), that becomes a maintenance issue.
**Partly.** Safety owns the event. You coordinate the damage repair.
**Rarely.** Sudden fuel-economy changes on one unit may be worth a maintenance look.
**Yes.** Meters drive PM schedules, and can sync to systems such as Fleetio.

callout.title: Avoid alert fatigue
callout.text: If every alert pings you, you'll start ignoring all of them. Work with your manager on which alert rules go to maintenance, such as active engine faults and DVIR defects, and which go to safety or dispatch.

timeline.title: Alert arrives
timeline.text: For example "Engine fault — T-311". Note the time, unit, code and location.

timeline.title: Read the details
timeline.text: Look at the fault description, any suggested action steps, whether it's still active, and the history: has this happened before?

timeline.title: Contact the driver
timeline.text: Ask about warning lamps, symptoms and power. A red stop lamp, low air or overheating means stop safely.

timeline.title: Decide urgency
timeline.text: Stop now, repair today, or schedule. Check HOS remaining and the load.

timeline.title: Arrange service
timeline.text: Use the location to pick a nearby qualified shop or mobile tech, and tell dispatch.

timeline.title: Record it
timeline.text: Open or update the work order or case in your maintenance system. It may be Samsara's own maintenance tools or a connected system like Fleetio.

timeline.title: Confirm and close
timeline.text: After the repair, confirm the fault is no longer active and close the loop with the driver and dispatch.

what: **ProTransport** (often written "Pro Transport") is trucking software made by **RTS**, a company that also offers factoring and other services to trucking companies. RTS describes it as a [[TMS]] for fleets "from one to 500 trucks", with an Enterprise version for high-volume fleets and freight brokerages.

callout.title: Which "Pro Transport"?
callout.text: Several unrelated businesses use similar names. This page covers **ProTransport by RTS** (rtsinc.com) and only the features RTS lists on its official pages. Companies buy different plans and integrations, so check what your employer actually uses.

what: Where Fleetio is the *maintenance* system and Samsara is the *telematics* system, a TMS is the **operations and money** system: which load goes on which truck with which driver, and how it gets billed and paid.

tiles.title: Run dispatch
tiles.text: Loads are planned and assigned from a dispatch board or scheduler.

tiles.title: Stay connected to drivers
tiles.text: Drivers get trip assignments and send status updates from a mobile app.

tiles.title: Keep documents with the load
tiles.text: Load paperwork photographed by drivers is attached to the right load.

tiles.title: Get paid and pay drivers
tiles.text: Invoices, payments, statements, driver pay statements and QuickBooks export.

how: Everything in a TMS revolves around the **load**. A load is created, given a driver and truck, tracked through status updates, delivered, documented and billed.

When the driver updates the trip status in the Driver Mobile App, RTS says the update appears on the dispatcher's **dispatch board** right away, without manual entry. Documents the driver photographs are attached to the correct load, so billing can invoice without waiting for paper.

callout.title: About tracking
callout.text: In ProTransport, "tracking" means **trip status updates** from the driver app and **load status alerts** to brokers. RTS also lists integrations with ELD providers. What location data comes in depends on the provider your company connects, so ask before you assume.

example: **Example fleet (fictional): 35 trucks, dry van, mostly brokered freight.**

dialog: 08:00 — Dispatch scans a rate confirmation for load 77120 (Chicago → Columbus). The details fill in.
08:15 — The load is assigned to driver Ana on truck T-122. Ana gets a trip assignment notification in the app.
13:40 — Ana updates the status to "Loaded". The dispatch board updates and the broker gets a load status alert.
Maintenance, heads up: T-122 is on 77120, delivering in Columbus tomorrow 07:00. Its safety & maintenance reminder shows the annual inspection is due next week.
Thanks. I'll book the inspection near our Columbus shop after delivery, so it doesn't touch the load.
Next day 07:30 — Ana photographs the signed BOL in the app. It's attached to load 77120 and billing invoices it.

what: **Thermo King** is not mainly a software company. It makes **equipment**: transport refrigeration and temperature-control systems. It is a brand of **Trane Technologies**, and dates its start to **1938**, when co-founder **Frederick McKinley Jones** designed a mechanical refrigeration unit for trucks. Thermo King's products today cover vans, trucks, trailers, rail and containers.

callout.title: What is a TRU?
callout.text: A **transport refrigeration unit (TRU)** is a self-contained cooling and heating system mounted on a trailer, usually on the front wall, or on a truck body. Many trailer TRUs have their own small diesel engine and fuel tank. Hybrid-electric models, such as Thermo King's Precedent S-750i, can also plug into shore power.

why: Food, medicine, flowers and some chemicals must stay within a temperature range from pickup to delivery. A [[Reefer]] trailer is an insulated box, but insulation only slows heat down. The TRU actively **removes heat** (or adds it in cold weather) to hold the **setpoint**.

how: Every TRU uses the same basic physics as a household refrigerator: refrigerant **absorbs heat inside** the box and **releases it outside**.

how.title: The refrigeration cycle (simplified)

pins.d: Squeezes low-pressure refrigerant gas into hot, high-pressure gas.
Fans blow outside air across it. The refrigerant gives off heat and condenses to a liquid.
Drops the pressure so the liquid becomes very cold.
Cargo air is blown across it. The refrigerant absorbs that heat and boils back to gas, then returns to the compressor.

how.note: Generic vapor-compression cycle — not a specific Thermo King model. Real units add valves, heat and defrost circuits and controls.

how: The **controller** compares the sensor readings to the setpoint and switches between cooling, null and heating to hold it. **Defrost** periodically warms the evaporator coil to melt ice. The SR-4 starts it on a timer (programmable intervals of 2, 4, 6, 8 or 12 hours) or *on demand* when the return air, discharge air and coil temperatures show icing. A driver can also start it manually.

visual.title: How air moves through a loaded reefer
